fields.foundation: The French colonial enterprise began with exploration rather than settlement. Jacques Cartier reached the Gulf of St. Lawrence in 1534, claiming territory for Francis I, but decades of religious civil war prevented meaningful colonisation. The first colonial empire took root only in 1608, when Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec as the capital of New France and the centre of the fur trade. Jean-Baptiste Colbert, Louis XIV's chief minister for finance and the navy, then made expansion a matter of economic policy, establishing the French East India Company in 1664 and building a powerful fleet. The western part of Hispaniola, Saint-Domingue, passed formally to France in 1697 and became the most profitable sugar colony in the Caribbean. By around 1710, the first empire stretched from Acadia along the St. Lawrence through the Great Lakes and down the Mississippi to Louisiana, covering some ten million square kilometres. The Seven Years' War destroyed it. The 1763 Treaty of Paris forced France to cede Canada and all North American territory east of the Mississippi to Britain, leaving it with Caribbean islands, Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, and five Indian trading posts. A second empire, begun with the 1830 invasion of Algiers, eventually surpassed the first by every measure.
fields.socioeconomy: The economy of the first empire rested on mercantilism and plantation slavery. By the 1780s Saint-Domingue alone produced around forty percent of the sugar and some sixty percent of the coffee consumed in Europe, making it the most lucrative colony in the world. The second empire operated on a different model, combining resource extraction with administrative integration. Algeria, organised into French departments from 1848, attracted around one million European settlers, the pieds-noirs. The result was a dual economy in which European landowners dominated export agriculture while indigenous Algerians worked marginal land under legal discrimination. Across the empire, the doctrine of mise en valeur directed colonial economies towards producing raw materials for French industry: rubber from Indochina, phosphates from North Africa, groundnuts from Senegal, cotton from the Sahel. The indigénat legal regime imposed a separate and inferior status on colonial subjects, institutionalising economic exclusion and forced labour. The empire was presented as a mission civilisatrice, which obscured a largely extractive relationship. French republican intellectuals struggled increasingly to rationalise the contradiction as the twentieth century advanced.
fields.military: French imperial military power was built on naval strength and specialised colonial forces. Colbert's naval construction programme made France one of the leading maritime powers of Europe by the late seventeenth century and allowed it to project force across the oceans. The loss of naval supremacy to Britain, confirmed at the Battle of Lagos and at Quiberon Bay in 1759, was the proximate military cause of the first empire's collapse. The second empire relied heavily on the Foreign Legion, founded in 1831, and the tirailleurs, colonial infantry recruited from Senegal, Algeria, Indochina, and elsewhere, who fought in both world wars and whose pay and pensions lagged far behind those of their French counterparts. Under Napoleon III, colonial campaigns added Cochinchina, New Caledonia, and an expanded Senegal under Louis Faidherbe, and the Third Republic later pushed into Tunisia, Tonkin, Madagascar, and the Sahel. The catastrophic defeat that broke the second empire came at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954, where General Vo Nguyen Giap's Viet Minh besieged a French garrison and forced its surrender after fifty-six days. It was the most consequential colonial military defeat of the twentieth century. The Algerian War that followed cost an estimated 300,000 to 1.5 million Algerian lives across eight years. It confirmed that no military solution existed for a colonial relationship the subject population had decided to end.
fields.governance: France governed its two empires through different models. The first empire relied on chartered companies, appointed governors, and trading monopolies loosely supervised from Versailles, with little institutional coherence. The second empire developed a more systematic apparatus. Algeria was governed as an extension of France itself after 1848, with departments, prefects, and French civil law applying to European settlers while most indigenous Algerians remained under the indigénat. Indochina was administered as five distinct territories under a governor-general, based in Hanoi from 1902. West and Equatorial Africa were organised into two large federations headquartered at Dakar and Brazzaville. The 1946 constitution attempted to reframe this system as the French Union, extending citizenship to colonial subjects and granting limited representation in Paris, but the reform was applied inconsistently and satisfied almost no one. De Gaulle's French Community of 1958 offered autonomy within a French framework. Guinea under Sékou Touré rejected it outright and took immediate independence, and within two years the remaining African territories had followed, which dissolved the whole administrative structure.
fields.impact: The French Empire's most durable legacy is linguistic and institutional. French remains an official language in twenty-nine countries, more than any language except English. The Napoleonic Code, exported across continental Europe during Napoleon's brief continental dominance, fundamentally shaped the legal systems of France's European neighbours and, through them and through French colonial rule, those of states across Africa and the Americas. French educational institutions of the colonial period produced the post-independence leadership class of much of Francophone Africa, and the close networks between Paris and these elites, known as Françafrique, shaped African politics long after formal decolonisation. The Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804 destroyed Saint-Domingue and produced the first Black republic in history under the leadership of Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines. It was a direct consequence of the first empire's plantation economy and a turning point in Atlantic history.
fields.decline: The first empire collapsed through military defeat in 1763 and the loss of its richest colony in the Haitian Revolution. The second empire was dissolved by nationalist resistance that the French state could not suppress without costs that democratic public opinion would not bear. Dien Bien Phu in 1954 ended French Indochina; Morocco and Tunisia gained independence in 1956; fourteen sub-Saharan colonies and trust territories became independent in 1960; and the Évian Accords of March 1962 brought Algerian independence after eight years of war. Vanuatu's independence in 1980 completed the process. Unlike empires dissolved by external conquest, the French colonial empire collapsed because the contradiction between France's republican identity and its colonial practice could not in the end be resolved.
fields.summary: The French Empire followed a double arc that is rare among modern empires: it collapsed, was rebuilt, and peaked again at greater scale. It was then undone not by a rival power but by the incompatibility of its own values with its own conduct.
fields.teaser: France's imperial ambitions peaked first under Napoleon, who redrew the map of Europe, and again in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when France built the world's second-largest colonial empire.
fields.t0: France built two colonial empires: one in North America and the Caribbean, lost in 1763, and a larger one in Africa and Asia.
fields.t1: Plantation slavery made Saint-Domingue the world's richest colony, while the later empire extracted raw materials for French industry.
fields.t2: Nationalist wars from Dien Bien Phu to Algeria ended it, leaving French as an official language in twenty-nine countries.
fields.dyk: By the 1780s Saint-Domingue, now Haiti, produced around 40 per cent of Europe's sugar and some 60 per cent of its coffee.
